title: How do you design a delayed job scheduler at scale: why NOT poll the DB every second (`SELECT ... WHERE execute_at <= NOW()`), and instead use time bucketing / a Redis sorted set (score = execute-at timestamp) to find due jobs efficiently?
shortTitle: How do you design a delayed job scheduler at scale?
keyPoints: Polling a DB every second wastes queries, loads the database, and causes claim contention among workers.
A Redis sorted set with execute-at timestamp as score makes finding due jobs a single O(log N + K) range query.
Jobs scheduled for the future cost nothing to skip because the structure is ordered.
Atomic claim via a Lua script (ZRANGEBYSCORE + ZREM) prevents two workers from running the same job.
Time bucketing partitions jobs into per-minute keys so each tick inspects only the current bucket.
Shard a hot bucket by hash(jobId) % N to spread load across workers.
For durability, keep authoritative job definitions in a relational store and use Redis as the fast time index.

s1_definition.oneliner: Do not poll the whole database every second for due jobs; store jobs ordered by execute-at in a Redis sorted set so finding due jobs is one range query, and bucket by time so each tick inspects only the relevant slice.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **DB polling problem** – most polls return nothing (wasted work), the query loads the database, and multiple workers fight over the same due rows.
- **Redis sorted set** – ZADD with execute-at as score; ZRANGEBYSCORE -inf NOW returns only due jobs in O(log N + K) time.
- **Atomic claim** – a Lua script does ZRANGEBYSCORE + ZREM in one atomic operation so no two workers grab the same job.
- **Time bucketing** – partition jobs into per-minute keys so each tick only looks at the current bucket.
- **Sharding hot buckets** – hash(jobId) % N spreads a busy minute across N partitions.
- **Durability** – Redis persistence + relational store as source of truth + periodic reconciliation.
s1_definition.analogy: The naive clerk walks the entire filing cabinet every second asking 'anything due?' The smart design files tasks in order of when they are due. The clerk glances at the front and pulls only the due ones. Time bucketing: one pigeonhole per minute, so at 10:05 the clerk opens only the 10:05 pigeonhole.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  DB Polling vs Redis Sorted Set

  DB Polling (every second)
  ┌──────────┐  SELECT  ┌──────────┐
  │ Worker 1 │ ──────── │          │
  │ Worker 2 │ ──────── │    DB    │  lock contention!
  │ Worker 3 │ ──────── │          │  mostly empty results
  └──────────┘          └──────────┘

  Redis Sorted Set
  ┌──────────┐  ZRANGEBYSCORE  ┌──────────┐
  │ Worker   │ ──────────────► │  Redis   │
  └──────────┘  + Lua ZREM     │ Sorted   │
                (atomic claim)  │ Set      │
                               └──────────┘
                Only due jobs returned; future jobs skipped

  Time Bucketing
  ┌───────────┐ ┌───────────┐ ┌───────────┐
  │ 10:03     │ │ 10:04     │ │ 10:05     │ ← current bucket
  │ (done)    │ │ (done)    │ │ inspect!  │
  └───────────┘ └───────────┘ └───────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A delayed job scheduler runs work at a future time. The naive design polls a database every second, but at scale this wastes queries (most return nothing), loads the database, and causes lock contention when workers fight over the same due rows.

The scalable design stores jobs in a Redis sorted set with the execute-at timestamp as the score. Finding due jobs is a single ZRANGEBYSCORE range query that returns only past-due jobs and skips millions of future ones. An atomic Lua script (ZRANGEBYSCORE + ZREM) prevents two workers from claiming the same job. Time bucketing partitions jobs into per-minute keys so each tick inspects only the current bucket, and sharding a hot bucket by hash(jobId) spreads load across parallel workers.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj used this to schedule millions of reminders and hold expirations after per-second DB polling started loading the database. Due jobs accumulate during any scheduler outage and are picked up naturally on recovery.

Remember one sentence: do not poll the whole database every second; store jobs ordered by execute-at in a Redis sorted set so finding due jobs is one cheap range query, claim atomically with a Lua script, and bucket by time so each tick inspects only the relevant slice.
